activities.anchor: Robert Hooke sliced a piece of cork
activities.caption: rebuild the discovery timeline — cork to cell theory
activities.name: csHistoryOrder

config.prompt: From a slice of cork to a law with no exceptions — put the history in order:
items: 1665: Robert Hooke slices cork and sees a honeycomb of tiny empty boxes
He borrows the word 'cell' from the small rooms monks sleep in
1670s: van Leeuwenhoek looks at pond water — the boxes are alive and swimming
Almost 200 years later: cell theory's three rules are agreed
In all the years since, no exception has ever been found
config.why: Everything alive is made of cells; the cell is the basic unit of life; every cell comes from another cell — the three rules that survived every microscope since.

activities.anchor: Plant cells have three extra parts
activities.caption: pair each part with its everyday job
activities.name: csJobsMatch

config.prompt: Every part has a job you already understand — pair them:

pairs.left: the bag itself — a skin two molecules thick, dotted with tiny doors
the library holding the full instruction manual
the power stations, earning the cell's money
tiny specks that read the copies and build proteins
a water balloon pressing everything outward

config.why: ATP is the cell's money — mitochondria earn it and every other part spends it. A full vacuole is the difference between crisp lettuce and wilted lettuce.

activities.anchor: The whole ladder repeats one pattern
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the divide-by-a-thousand ladder
activities.name: csLadderCloze

config.text: Divide a metre by 1,000 → a %%0%% (mm), about the width of your fingernail. Divide again by 1,000 → a %%1%% (μm). Divide again by 1,000 → a %%2%% (nm), a billionth of a metre.
config.hint: Each rung of the ladder repeats one pattern: divide by a thousand.

activities.caption: pin a human cell on the micrometre scale
activities.name: csCellPlace

config.prompt: A hair is about 70 μm across. Place a typical human cell on the scale (μm):
config.why: 10–30 μm — bigger than a bacterium (1–5 μm), ten times bigger than a virus (about 100 nm).
config.context: A normal school microscope that shows bacteria clearly cannot see viruses at all.

activities.anchor: And there is a physical ceiling
activities.caption: true or false — zoom, resolution and light
activities.name: csResolutionJudge

statements.s: A light microscope cannot separate two points closer than about 200 nm.
statements.why: Visible light travels in waves roughly that size — that is the ceiling.

statements.s: Zooming a light microscope in enough will eventually reveal ribosomes.
statements.why: Magnification only enlarges — a bigger blur, not more structure.

statements.s: An electron microscope uses beams of electrons instead of light.
statements.why: That is how you see inside a cell — the ribosomes, the membrane layers.

statements.s: Resolution and magnification are the same measurement.
statements.why: Resolution is the physical limit set by light's wavelength; magnification just scales the image.

activities.anchor: a book locked in a vault builds nothing
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the supply-chain answer
activities.name: csVaultSpot

config.prompt: This protein-synthesis answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The nucleus keeps DNA safe — but a book locked in a vault builds nothing.
The vault makes a disposable photocopy of one page (one gene) and ships it out.
The photocopy is called messenger RNA.
The ribosome reads the copy three letters at a time, each triplet selecting one amino acid.
The DNA itself travels out through the pores to do the building.
config.correction: DNA never leaves the vault — only the disposable mRNA copies travel out; the blueprint stays.
config.why: The blueprint stays; the photocopy travels — one human cell runs this supply chain for about 20,000 different genes at the same time.

activities.anchor: Here is a classic exam skill, done slowly
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the drawing's magnification
activities.name: csDrawEstimate

config.prompt: The real cell is 30 μm long; you draw it 60 mm long in your notebook. How magnified is the drawing?
config.why: 60 mm = 60,000 μm; 60,000 ÷ 30 = ×2,000 — and the microscope's ×400 was already divided out by the calibration.
config.context: Three magnifications were in play — the microscope's, the calibration's, and the drawing's — each answering a different question.

activities.anchor: There are also two great cell empires
activities.caption: two empires — drag between them
activities.name: csEmpiresCompare

config.prompt: The two great cell empires — drag the divider:

before.label: eukaryotic (ours)
before.text: DNA kept in a nucleus, with the work divided among membrane-bound compartments — the merged empire.

after.label: prokaryotic (bacteria)
after.text: Smaller and simpler: no nucleus — circular DNA floats in the cytoplasm, often with extra plasmid rings; ribosomes and walls chemically different enough for antibiotics to exploit.

config.why: The deepest surprise: mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria another cell swallowed and kept — still carrying their own circular DNA and double membranes (Margulis's endosymbiosis).
